problem:
The second-order differential equation $3{y}^{″}+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$

examples.problem:
The second-order differential equation $y'' + 5y' - 2y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/59e386be8b30fca475a2e0d164687a6561b9ab368b9879fc301d328896d184fd.png)
Find the matrix $A.$
examples.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

$$
y''= -5y' + 2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y'' = -5x_2 + 2x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=2{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/f35de5e6f066144c4130e38304abbff552730dc1fe97828572a66e68970c5d52.png)

Hence, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/314f9dcf277b61dac9985c448aed98113516592e3822cc47a8566d28a480651b.png)

feedback.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}+3{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}-12y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1,\,{y}^{″}(0)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(0)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q+r)\cdot f(t).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {y}^{″}(0) & ={x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+12y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}+12{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=1,r=3,f(t)=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q+r)\cdot f(t) & =(2-1+3)(12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =4(12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$
